context: a letter from J. D. Hooker, which you are answering
exchanges:
I forgot to tell you that Currey asked me to ask you, what you wished about the execution of the woodcuts,— he says there was something unsatisfactory about the last. Will you write straight to him about them

F. Currey Esq

3 New Square   Lincolns Inn

W. C.

he wants to put them in hand at once.

Thomson has gone over Scott’s paper. & the enclosed is his conclusion; he is a scientific arithmetician & would I am sure solve the difficulty if soluble; the Denominators are obviously arbitrary & useless.

I have read through Scott’s paper, & am amazed at his industry & ability, but in its present state the paper is not fit for publication, & I think the experiments should have been repeated— his discord with Gærtner either shakes the whole value of his system of experimentation, or shows that similar experiments give different results, or that one of the observers is wrong.

You are the only judge of the value of such a paper:— it is awfully tedious to read. Much of it is simply a repetition of the Tables, & that part might be shortened—perhaps.

Ever yrs affec | Jos D Hooker

I return Scotts’ paper.

Currey wants to know, who you would wish to execute the wood engravings—

See that proofs are sent to you of them

Thanks for your note, & very many thanks about Scott’s paper. Give Thomson my best thanks; you & he have relieved me from much doubt, & I have returned Scott his paper with proper advice & explanations.— I received a few days ago a letter from him, with a flourishing account of his prospects & full of gratitude. He sends messages to you & Thomson, which I enclose instead of copying.—

On getting your note I wrote to Mr. Currey about woodcuts & told him I would pay for them.—

I did so thoroughily enjoy your visit my dear old friend, & it did me no harm.— It was high luck being so well, for I have had no such brilliant days before or since.—

My life is as uniform as that of a mill-horse; my sole work being the grinding & polishing of badly written sentences.— You did not take Heer’s pamphlet, & I do not suppose you care to have it sent.—

Farewell | Yours affectly. | C. Darwin
